t71a_sp5p2z1: Does saying it make the memory fiction? Well, no. It's still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details are fuzzy, and nobody's off the hook either (any repair that's owed is still owed). Keep an ear on the narrator, though. If they start to sneer, stop. Stop too if you feel more ashamed, or kind of unreal, since telling it from farther away won't fix that. When it does help, let it stay one line, and maybe ask the younger you in that story what they need from you now.
t71a_jwa: If talking or picturing gets you nothing but silence, try paper. Write with your wrong hand, the clumsy one whose letters already look like a first grader's, and put down whatever scared or hurt feelings are really there (no making things up for your little one). Then answer with your good hand, as the grown-up, doing whichever of its three jobs is needed. Does the protective part grab the pen first? Then it gets the wrong hand first, until it's had its say, and your little one can wait their turn.
t71a_jwb: Sometimes you ask and get silence, and then you're just sitting there wondering if you're doing it wrong. Try writing instead, with your wrong hand, the clumsy one whose letters already look like a little kid's. Whatever scared or hurt feelings are really there go on the page, nothing invented. Your good hand writes back as the grown-up, doing whichever of its three jobs is needed. And if the protective part shows up first, it gets the clumsy hand and its say before anyone asks your little one for theirs.
t71a_jw2a: And if writing it all out just makes everything murkier, skip the meaning-making while you write. A few dated facts will do, like what happened and what helped, or a voice note on your phone, whatever keeps track of things. Patterns can wait until later, if they turn out to matter. A memory aid gets to be as dull as a grocery list.
t71a_jw2b: If writing about your feelings ties you in knots, there's a lower-tech version too. Jot the date and what helped, or just leave yourself a voice note. Nobody has to work out what it all means while they're writing it. Patterns can show up later, if they show up at all, and a memory aid doesn't have to explain your life to do its job.
t71a_oia: Mornings get one small intention, something like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Just the one. At night you look back over the day with the kind eyes of a friend reading over your shoulder. Where did you catch the hook? Where did it run the whole routine anyway, before you noticed? And what's the next small repair, or the next thing you could do to protect your little one?
t71a_oib: Here's a simple one. In the morning, set one small intention, like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." At night, go over the day without putting yourself on trial: where you caught the hook, and where it ran its whole routine anyway (you'll probably find both). Then think of the next small repair, or something that would protect your little one a bit more tomorrow.
t71a_jl2a: Regular breathing is fine for this, nothing fancy. It isn't asking you to forgive whoever hurt you either, or to picture their sad childhood. Calling them up is a whole separate decision, one for a day when you're less flooded. What it can do is take off some weight, that idea that feeling this proves you're the broken one, when plenty of people are feeling it right along with you.
t71a_jl2b: You don't need any special breathing. And forgiving whoever hurt you, or imagining their childhood? Also not required, and neither is getting in touch with them (if that ever happens, it's its own decision, made on a calmer day than this). The point is just to stop treating a feeling this many people have had as proof that you, specifically, are defective.
t71a_cs1a: Every session needs a real ending, or the processing just keeps going, and that can turn into one more way to avoid living. So look around and say where you are, even if it's only "my living room, the cat's here." Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair holding you up. Your jaw and hands have probably been clenching this whole time, so let them go.
t71a_cs1b: When you're done, end it for real. Otherwise processing can go on and on, until it's just another way to not live your life. Take a look around and name where you are (yes, out loud, even if it feels silly). Then feel something solid, your feet on the floor or the chair under you, and unclench your jaw and your hands, which have probably been at it this whole time.

## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

Does saying it make the memory fiction? Well, no, it's still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details turn out fuzzy. And nobody's off the hook (you included, if you were the one who did it): whatever repair is owed is still owed. If the line helps, keep it to the one line.
